newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian ministers begin 1997 budget review.
newsitem.headline: Italian ministers begin 1997 budget review.

text.p: Ministers charged with drafting Italy's key 1997 budget package began talks with cabinet colleagues on Tuesday on how to pare spending.
The team of troubleshooters, led by Treasury and Budget Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi, met first with Labour Minister Tiziano Treu and state pensions fund chief Gianni Billia.
None of the participants made any comment to reporters at the end of the session, the first of a series to review spending plans by individual ministries.
The team also includes Finance Minister Vincenzo Visco and Prime Minister Romano Prodi's top aide Enrico Micheli.
Government officials said they would meet separately with the ministers of transport, defence and posts and telecommunications later in the day.
Under Italian law, the budget package must be presented to parliament by September 30. Both chambers then have until December 31 to approve it.

Prodi's centre-left government is aiming to cut the public sector borrowing requirement by 32.4 trillion lire ($21.39 billion) in 1997. Two thirds of this is due to come from spending cuts and the remainder from increased revenue.

Commentators say the government faces a tricky balancing act between measures strigent enough to please financial markets and signal Italy's commitment to joining a single European currency while keeping its key hard-left allies happy in parliament.
Prodi's government, elected in April, requires the support of the hard-left Communist Refoundation party in the lower house of parliament to obtain a majority.

For Prodi, the battle over the budget will be played out against a background of a slowing Italian economy and threats by union leaders of strikes this autumn as they renegotiate wage contracts with industrial employers.

Previous pledges not to touch Italy's two biggest areas of expenditure -- pensions and healthcare -- make the task even Commentators have said the budget will include big cuts in subsidies for state companies, a crackdown on excess spending by ministries and a new campaign to stamp out tax evasion.
Many cuts have been agreed but newspapers said the last six to seven trillion lire were proving difficult to find. -- Rome newsroom +39 6 6782501 ($1=1515 Lire)
